title: Light Speed Stop 6: Saturn's Dying Rings
topic: Light-speed journey stop 6: Saturn (~67 light-minutes at closest; rings about 280,000 km wide but mostly only ~10 m thick; mostly water ice; ring rain drains them; may vanish in ~100-300 million years; less dense than water; Titan and Enceladus)
links_to_previous: Answers episode 5's cliffhanger (will Saturn's rings vanish?): yes, eventually. The journey continues from Jupiter to Saturn, then heads for Uranus and Neptune.

summary: Answer: yes, the rings will vanish. ~67 light-minutes at closest. Rings span ~280,000 km but are mostly only ~10 m thick, mostly water ice. Ring material rains into Saturn; scientists think they could be gone in 100-300 million years. Saturn is less dense than water. Next stop: Uranus and Neptune.

scenes.narration: Saturn's rings are disappearing right now.
The answer: yes. Scientists think they'll be gone in a few hundred million years.
At its closest, light from Earth needs about sixty-seven minutes to get here.
The rings stretch about two hundred eighty thousand kilometers across.
Yet they're mostly just ten meters thick. Thinner than a house.
They're made almost entirely of water ice, from dust grains to house-sized chunks.
Gravity is pulling them in. The ice falls into Saturn like rain.
Saturn is so light, it would float in a giant bathtub.
Its moon Enceladus shoots icy geysers into space.
And Titan has lakes, but filled with liquid methane, not water.
Farther out, two ice giants hide something even stranger.
Next stop, Uranus and Neptune. Does it rain diamonds there? Yes or no?
